transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-31 16:00 PDT
- Duration: ~43 minutes
- Attendees: Emma M, Rohit S, Jules C (Redwood) — Aisha K, Tom R, Marta L (LumenWell)

Auto-summary (auto): Demo focused on hosted API chat basics + resilience patterns; security questions; pilot agreement.

Transcript:
[00:00] Emma Martinez: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I'm Emma from Redwood, I'm the AE on this. We'll do a quick 30-minute demo and then leave room for questions and the pilot next steps. Rohit is our SE.
[00:22] Aisha Khan: Hi thanks, we only have about an hour total, so appreciate keeping it tight. Our main goals are low tail latency for interactive assist and strict data controls, plus predictable cost.
[00:35] Rohit Singh: Great, quick confirmation: are you running most inference in region us-west-2? And what's your existing stack — are you calling external APIs from our backend or client-side?
[00:48] Tom Reed: We're primarily in us-west-2, server-side calls via an internal API gateway. Right now we call a managed model from CloudAIX but tail latency spikes and costs are killing us.
[01:05] Rohit Singh: Got it. We'll show hosted Red­wood API behavior and options: streaming responses, typical parameters, retry semantics, and our graceful degradation — like model fallback and token limit strategies.
[01:22] Marta Lopez: Also curious about key management — we need to use our KMS and ensure logs are only audit-level not storing PII.
[01:30] Emma Martinez: Yep that'll come up in the security pack. We'll note KMS and retention settings.

--- Demo start ---
[02:05] Rohit Singh: I'm sharing my screen, starting from a quick cURL request to our /chat endpoint. Example payload: messages, model (we'll pick rdx-std-8k), stream=true. Watch the streaming chunks come back with partial tokens.
[02:30] Speaker 4: (inaudible) the stream... I'm not seeing the chunking — is it chunked by token or by chunk size?
[02:38] Rohit Singh: Good question — streaming is chunked by the runtime's flush policy which is a combination of token thresholds and timing, so small messages flush quickly for low-latency. For high throughput you can tune chunk_size and use the console suggestion to increase batch windows.
[03:05] Aisha Khan: If a stream fails mid response, do you re-send from the beginning or do you support resume?
[03:12] Rohit Singh: Currently we don't resume partial token streams at the protocol level, the common pattern is to craft the client to re-request with an idempotency_key and the same conversation history; Redwood supports idempotency keys at the request layer to avoid double billing and duplicate side effects. We also provide partial response caching for prefix reuse which helps in many use cases.
[03:40] Tom Reed: What about retries — exponential backoff or linear? Any recommended parameters?
[03:47] Rohit Singh: Exponential backoff is recommended; our SDKs expose a retry helper with jitter. Typical defaults: initial 200ms, multiplier 2x, max 3 retries. For streaming use cases, often you reduce retries to 1-2 and rely more on fallback models to preserve UX.
[04:10] Aisha Khan: Fallback models meaning lower-cost smaller models?
[04:15] Rohit Singh: Exactly — fallback to rdx-lite or a quantized variant. The console Optimize tab will recommend a quantization profile and show estimated token-cost savings.
[04:30] Emma Martinez: Quick tour of the Console — here's per-route latency percentiles, token-cost breakdown, and a rollout config that pins a canary model to 5% traffic. You can set fallback policy per route: e.g., on 5xx use model variant X, on high-latency routes route to another region.
[05:00] Marta Lopez: Do you allow region restrictions so data never leaves EU?
[05:04] Rohit Singh: For hosted customers we have region controls and data residency options; for strict requirements we also offer private deployment (VPC/on-prem). We'll include region SLA info in the security pack.

[06:20] Rohit Singh: Back to params — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences. For deterministic templates we recommend temperature=0 and max_tokens constrained. For freer generation, temp 0.6 and top_p 0.9. The console also surfaces traffic-aware suggestions — e.g., reduce max_tokens for chat summaries to save cost.
[06:50] Aisha Khan: Do you support per-token streaming costs visible? We need to show billing to product teams.
[06:55] Emma Martinez: Yes, the billing UI shows token-per-call and granular breakdown by model and route; you can export CSVs for cost allocation.

[08:00] Rohit Singh: Now demo a small failure scenario: I'll intentionally drop the connection after the stream starts.
[08:12] (sound of keyboard)
[08:18] Rohit Singh: Connection dropped, client logs show incomplete response. Client triggers retry with the same idempotency_key — on our side, the request is recognized as duplicate and either returns cached completed response if available or triggers fallback to a smaller model to get at least a partial answer quickly.
[08:45] Tom Reed: So we can trade final accuracy for responsiveness — that's nice. How do you measure quality regressions when switching models?
[08:55] Jules Carter: We bake evals into Optimize — you can run prompt sets and get quality regression alerts. During rollout you can require quality gates, and the console will auto-roll back if drift exceeds thresholds.
[09:15] Aisha Khan: Any limits on KV-cache sizes? We have long multi-turn contexts — up to ~12k tokens.
[09:23] Rohit Singh: Our runtime supports extended KV cache up to model context limits; for hosts using shorter models we do prefix caching to stitch replies. Watch out for memory/latency tradeoffs — Optimize will suggest quantization or switching to a 32k context model for large histories.

[10:40] Marta Lopez: Security — can you integrate with our SSO (SAML) and provide RBAC for routes?
[10:46] Emma Martinez: Yes, SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC are supported for enterprise plans. Audit logs include per-request metadata, and you can set retention policies. We'll attach the SOC2 attestation and encryption-in-transit and at-rest docs.

[12:00] Rohit Singh: Quick code snippet for streaming reconnection in JS: open eventsource/websocket, handle partial chunks, if disconnected call PATCH /session or re-POST with idempotency_key and recon in the client. Our SDK has a helper to manage that.
[12:28] Speaker 4: We have mobile clients — any difference?
[12:33] Rohit Singh: Mobile differences: unstable networks, so shorter streams with smaller flush thresholds work better. Also use client-side caching of last good response to show something while you reconnect.

[14:00] Aisha Khan: On pricing: if we run a pilot with 50k tokens/day, how do we estimate cost for fallback model traffic?
[14:08] Emma Martinez: We'll model it — but typical pattern is 90% main model, 10% fallback; console Optimize can simulate cost with your traffic mix. I'll include a 6-month pilot sketch in the next steps.

[15:30] Rohit Singh: Now a quick live example of parameter tuning. I'm sending identical prompts with temp 0, 0.5, and 1.0 and showing variance.
[15:45] (typing)
[15:52] Rohit Singh: Temp 0 returns much shorter deterministic output; temp 1.0 is more varied and sometimes hallucinates. For assistant flows we usually keep temp 0–0.3.
[16:20] Tom Reed: Any guardrails for hallucination?
[16:24] Rohit Singh: Safety layers: decoding constraints, token filters, and function-calling patterns where model returns structured data verified by deterministic checks. We also support post-generation reranking if needed.

[18:00] Emma Martinez: Another resilience pattern: circuit breaker thresholds in front of the model route. If latency > 500ms p95 for 2 minutes, return cached or a canned response and enqueue async processing. This keeps UX consistent.
[18:25] Marta Lopez: Can we set custom canned fallbacks per route?
[18:29] Emma Martinez: Yes, per-route fallbacks are configurable in the Console.

[19:40] Rohit Singh: A note on concurrency and batching: for chat with strict latency we recommend low concurrency per worker but small batch windows; Dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput if you have tight SLAs. Hosted is more cost-effective for variable usage.
[20:10] Aisha Khan: We're leaning hosted first for speed to market, but may move to dedicated as volume increases. Any migration friction?
[20:18] Emma Martinez: Minimal — same API surface and rollout configs. You pin model versions and switch to dedicated through the Console; our migration guide walks through VPC peering and private endpoints if you need it.

[22:00] Tom Reed: For logs and data retention — is raw input saved? We need to redact PHI.
[22:08] Rohit Singh: By default we log request metadata but you can opt out of storing content; for PHI we'd recommend private deployment or strict retention with customer-managed keys. We'll send a redaction / retention guide.

[23:45] Jules Carter: Quick tangent on Optimize: batching suggestions, quantization recommendations per model, and cost/latency tradeoff chart. You can run a simulated workload and Optimize returns recommended config and expected cost delta.
[24:20] Aisha Khan: Can Optimize run on our sample prompt set?
[24:25] Rohit Singh: Yes — during the pilot we'll run your prompt set and return tailored recommendations. That's part of the bench scripts.

[26:00] (short silence)
[26:12] Aisha Khan: One more thing — SLOs. We need 99.9 p50 and p95 below 400ms for the assistant. Feasible?
[26:20] Rohit Singh: 99.9 is aggressive for p50/p95 depending on model. For p50 sub-200ms on rdx-std variants is typical in us-west-2; p95 <400ms depends on payload sizes and caching. Dedicated capacity can deliver tighter percentiles. We'll include SLO numbers and a recommended config for your traffic shape.

[28:00] Emma Martinez: Ok wrapping up — recap and next steps.
[28:10] Emma Martinez: Action items: I'll send SOC2/security pack and pricing sketch; Rohit will send bench scripts and request a sample prompt set; Aisha to confirm pilot participants. We'll provision a sandbox org for you to run the week-long pilot.
[28:35] Aisha Khan: sounds good. Can we get a short note on the idempotency_key best practices?
[28:40] Rohit Singh: Yes — we'll include a short code example and recommended headers in the bench repo.
[29:00] Tom Reed: Great, thanks — overall this was helpful and I like the fallback ideas.
[29:10] Marta Lopez: Appreciate the security notes.
[29:15] Emma Martinez: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email and link the pilot kickoff calendar after Aisha confirms availability.
[29:25] (meeting ends, recording stops)
